'''Hellmuth Kneser''' (16 April 1898 – 23 August 1973) was a German [[mathematician]] who made notable contributions to [[group theory]] and [[topology]].  His most famous result may be his theorem on the existence of a [[prime decomposition (3-manifold)|prime decomposition for 3-manifolds]].  His proof originated the concept of [[normal surface]], a fundamental cornerstone of the theory of [[3-manifold]]s.

He was born in [[Dorpat]], [[Russian Empire]] (now [[Tartu]], [[Estonia]]) and died in [[Tübingen]], [[Germany]].  He was the son of the mathematician [[Adolf Kneser]] and the father of the mathematician [[Martin Kneser]].  He assisted [[Wilhelm Süss]] in the founding of the [[Mathematical Research Institute of Oberwolfach]] and served as the director of the institute from 1958 to 1959.
He was an editor of [[Mathematische Zeitschrift]], [[Archiv der Mathematik]] and [[Aequationes Mathematicae]].

Kneser formulated the problem of non-integer iteration of functions and proved the existence of the entire [[Abel function]] of the [[Exponential function|exponential]]; on the base of this Abel function, he constructed the [[functional square root]] of the exponential function as a half-iteration of the exponential, i.e. a function {{mvar|φ}} such that {{math|''φ''(''φ''(''z'')) {{=}} exp(''z'')}}.<ref name="sqrtexp">{{cite journal
|author=H.Kneser
|title=Reelle analytische Lösungen der Gleichung ''φ''(''φ''(''x''))&nbsp;=&nbsp;''e''<sup>''x''</sup> und verwandter Funktionalgleichungen
|journal=[[Journal für die reine und angewandte Mathematik]]
|url=http://resolver.sub.uni-goettingen.de/purl?GDZPPN002175851
|volume=187
|year=1950
|pages=56–67| doi=10.1515/crll.1950.187.56}}</ref>

Kneser was a student of [[David Hilbert]]. He was an advisor of a number of notable mathematicians, including [[Reinhold Baer]].

Hellmuth Kneser was a member of the [[NSDAP]] and also the [[Sturmabteilung|SA]].<ref>[http://litten.de/fulltext/cara.htm ''Die Carathéodory-Nachfolge in München 1938–1944''] by Freddy Litten</ref> In July 1934 he wrote to [[Ludwig Bieberbach]] a short note supporting his antisemitic views and stating: "May God grant German science a unitary, powerful and continued political position."<ref>Sanford L. Segal, [https://books.google.com/books?id=Xa8CNCyohBQC&pg=PA276 ''Mathematicians under the Nazis''], Princeton University Press, 2003, page 276</ref>
